paper_metadata.title: A Quantum Walk Model of Financial Options

summary: The paper proposes a discrete-time Hadamard-coin quantum walk model for European call option pricing on a 1-D log-price grid, using 100-step illustrative walks and 400-simulation ensemble averages with decoherence sigma_dec = 1. It reports a 6-month maturity example, 20% annualized volatility, 2% risk-free rate, seller/buyer margins of 10%/20%, and an implied-volatility moneyness mean of 0.988 with standard deviations 0.057 and about 0.1 from cited empirical studies.

experiments.description: Discrete-time quantum walk model used to price European-style call options, compared against the classical binomial/Jarrow-Rudd model and then combined with a quantum supply-and-demand model to produce market option prices and implied volatility/volume surfaces.

algorithm.variant: Hadamard-coin discrete-time quantum walk with optional decoherence and biased initial coin state
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Initial coin state set either to balanced superposition or slightly biased toward higher prices; biased case uses start angle 50 degrees.

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Position basis states |x_j⟩ represent discrete log-price levels on a 1-D grid; coin state controls left/right movement.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Compute European call option value V_n = ⟨ (1/(1+r)^n) [exp(S_n) - K]_+ ⟩ from the final quantum-walk probability distribution over log prices.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Decoherence can be introduced by perturbing the coin each step; market price model combines quantum and classical prices through a supply-demand compromise.

problem_instance.description: European-style call option pricing on a one-dimensional log-price grid, with illustrative figures for 100-step walks and 6-month maturity.

dataset_specification.description: Illustrative option-pricing setup; no market dataset used for the quantum-walk simulation itself.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Log-price interpretation of walk position; price increment adjusted to match target volatility; drift added for risk-free rate.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Analytical/numerical comparison of quantum vs classical distributions and option prices; figures show single runs and ensemble averages; no statistical test protocol reported.

implementation_details.classical_solver: classical binomial/Jarrow-Rudd model; classical supply-demand model
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Set option parameters (strike, volatility, risk-free rate, maturity); map walk position to log price; adjust grid/time step to match target variance.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Compute discounted expected payoff; derive implied volatility by inverting the classical binomial model; compute transaction volume from supply-demand propensity.

speedup_claims.conditions: for the ideal quantum walk without decoherence
speedup_claims.caveats: This is a property of the walk dynamics, not a demonstrated computational speedup for option pricing.

speedup_claims.conditions: if the time step is scaled to match final variance; quantum walk can be run on a quantum device
speedup_claims.caveats: No runtime benchmarks or asymptotic complexity analysis are provided.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Not explicitly stated; paper notes quantum walk can be implemented directly on a quantum computer and references speed advantages for certain classes of problem.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Not explicitly stated; classical binomial model implied.

advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: A quantum device capable of implementing a discrete-time quantum walk with Hadamard coin, optional decoherence, and position-space evolution; no qubit count or circuit resource estimate is given.
limiting_factors: No hardware execution or benchmark timings are reported

notes: No specific hardware or qubit count is reported; the paper states the model can be run directly on a quantum device and describes the walk abstractly, so num_qubits and hardware are not specified. The experiment is a theoretical/simulation study rather than a hardware run.
